introduction-its-not-just-a-job-title.core: SRE is a set of practices (SLOs, error budgets, toil reduction, blameless postmortems, engineering-driven operations) more than a job title. How an organisation structures SRE teams shapes whether those practices spread or become a renamed ops team. The main models are embedded, platform, consulting and hybrid, and each trades depth, scale and ownership differently.

first_principles.problem: A company renames its ops team 'SRE' but nothing changes: they still do manual deploys and get paged for every developer's bug.
truths: Reliability must be shared with developers.

analogy.title: A medical team structure
analogy.story: Whether specialists are embedded in each ward, run a central lab, or consult on request changes how care is delivered.
analogy.breaks: Hospitals have regulation; SRE models are chosen freely and change over time.

example.title: Renamed-ops smell test
flow: Do SREs write code > 50% of time?
Do services have SLOs + budget policy?
Can SRE hand back unreliable services?

check.q: What distinguishes real SRE from a renamed ops team?
check.a: Engineering-driven practices: SLOs and error budgets, capped toil with automation, shared ownership with developers, and blameless learning.

model-1-embedded-sre-the-co-pilot.core: Embedded SREs sit inside product teams, attending their stand-ups and planning, pairing on design, SLOs, observability and on-call. They get deep context and strong relationships and spread practices quickly. The risks are isolation from other SREs, inconsistency between teams, getting absorbed into feature work or becoming that team's ops person, and poor scaling, since SREs are scarce.

first_principles.problem: A critical payments team needs deep reliability expertise woven into daily development decisions.

analogy.title: A co-pilot in the cockpit
analogy.story: Present for every decision, deeply aware of the flight, but each plane needs its own.
analogy.breaks: Co-pilots are required on every flight; embeds are a choice for critical teams only.

example.title: Embed charter
flow: Goal: payments SLOs defined and met
SRE owns: SLOs, alerting, capacity reviews
Exit: team runs SLO reviews alone in 6 months

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Clear scope prevents becoming the team's ops person.

check.q: What's a common failure mode of embedded SRE?
check.a: The SRE becomes the team's dedicated ops person or feature developer, losing the SRE mandate and isolating them from SRE peers.

model-2-platform-sre-the-utility-provide.core: Platform SRE teams build and run shared infrastructure as products: Kubernetes platforms, CI/CD, observability stacks, databases-as-a-service, paved-road templates with SLOs and alerting built in. Product teams self-serve and own their services' reliability on top. This scales well and creates consistency, but platform teams can drift away from product needs and can't fix reliability problems inside application code.

first_principles.problem: Fifty product teams each run their own monitoring and deployment tooling inconsistently.
derivation: Offer **paved roads** with SLOs/observability built in.

analogy.title: A utility company
analogy.story: It provides reliable power and water to every house; homeowners still maintain their own appliances.
analogy.breaks: Utilities are regulated monopolies; platform teams must earn adoption.

example.title: Paved road
flow: Template: service with OTel, SLO, alerts, dashboards
Teams adopt; own their app SLOs

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Reliability defaults for every new service.

check.q: What's a key limitation of platform SRE?
check.a: It can't directly fix reliability problems in application code or design; product teams must own those.

model-3-consulting-sre-the-mercenaries.core: Consulting SREs work with product teams on engagements: production readiness reviews, defining SLOs, observability audits, capacity planning, postmortem facilitation, chaos GameDays. Then they move on, leaving the team more capable. It spreads expertise widely with few SREs and avoids long-term dependence, but advice can lack deep context and follow-through depends on the team's willingness.

first_principles.problem: A small SRE team must improve reliability across 80 services without becoming everyone's on-call.

analogy.title: Visiting specialists
analogy.story: A specialist assesses, prescribes and trains the local doctors, then visits the next hospital.
analogy.breaks: Patients must follow prescriptions; teams may not implement recommendations.

check.q: How does consulting SRE avoid creating long-term dependence?
check.a: Engagements are time-boxed and focus on teaching and leaving artifacts so the product team owns reliability afterwards.

the-anti-pattern-the-kitchen-sink-sre.core: The kitchen-sink SRE team becomes the catch-all for everything operational: tickets, manual deploys, access requests, on-call for every service, firefighting developers' bugs. Toil crowds out engineering, nothing gets automated, developers lose any incentive to build reliable software, and SREs burn out. The cure is explicit scope, toil caps, shared on-call, and the right to hand back services that don't meet standards.

first_principles.problem: SREs spend 90% of their time on tickets and pages, and attrition hits 40% in a year.
truths: Unbounded scope absorbs all ops work.
Ownership without authority burns people out.

analogy.title: The person who 'just helps out' with everything
analogy.story: Soon they're doing everyone's chores and have no time for their real job.
analogy.breaks: Helpful people can quit one task; organisations must change structure.

example.title: Hand-back policy
flow: SRE hands pager back to dev team

check.q: Why is the ability to 'hand back' a service important for SRE teams?
check.a: It keeps incentives aligned: developers must keep services reliable, preventing SRE from absorbing unlimited operational burden.

hybrid-models-combining-approaches.core: Most mature organisations mix models. A platform SRE team provides paved roads and observability; embedded SREs support the few most critical services; a consulting function runs readiness reviews and SLO programmes for everyone else; and product teams own their services' on-call with SRE as escalation. The mix evolves with scale, criticality and maturity.

first_principles.problem: A growing company finds no single SRE model fits both its critical payment systems and its long tail of internal tools.

analogy.title: A healthcare system
analogy.story: Public health programmes for all (platform), specialists for complex cases (embedded), and clinics offering check-ups (consulting).
analogy.breaks: Healthcare is funded by policy; SRE allocation follows business priorities.

example.title: Tiered allocation
flow: Tier 0 (payments, auth): embedded SRE, joint on-call
All: platform observability and SLO tooling

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Scarce SREs where they matter most.

example.outcome: SRE structure fitted to the business.

check.q: How do hybrid SRE models decide where to embed SREs?
check.a: By tiering services on business criticality and maturity, embedding only for the most critical services.
